biggestWin: Give running copy a measure ceiling and give the surface a line-breaking policy. Eight lines of CSS — `max-width` in `ch` on `.limit .t-small` and `.note .t-body`, `text-wrap: balance` on the short centred blocks and the card labels, `text-wrap: pretty` on the multi-line bodies — closes the 121-character line at 900px, the 97-character line at the declared 768 viewport, and all five one-word last lines at once. Everything else in the type system is already at the Vercel/Linear bar: nine roles, one computed signature each across seven states, four widths and both grounds, with leading and letterfit keyed to role on named ladders. Line-breaking is the one half of typesetting this surface has never been given, and it is the half that shows in the committed 768 frame.

findings.element: interaction-check.mjs:1231 and :1250 — the month/year guard and the banned-vocabulary guard
findings.problem: Both guards build their matcher with `new RegExp("\\\\b" + word + "\\\\b", ...)`. Read with `cat -A`, the file holds four literal backslashes, so the JS string value is `\\b` and the compiled pattern is `\\bsnapshot writer\\b` — a literal backslash followed by the letter b, not a word boundary. `main`'s innerText contains no backslash, so neither matcher can ever return a hit. Proven from a file (never through a shell, per lessons.md L-12): the gate's own expression, fed "The snapshot writer accrues structured periods for callers; the provider is the recorder." — every one of its seven banned terms — returns `[]`; the same expression with a surviving `\b` returns all seven. The month matcher, fed "This arrives in August and again in January." with both months bare, returns `[]`; corrected, it returns both. Each guard loops four states, so eight of the gate's 461 assertions cannot fail. This is exactly the L-12 trap the paid-for library names, and it has crept back into the guards for two round-1 confirmed findings: `august-inside-a-july-reading` and `refusals-written-in-the-studio-vocabulary`. Both are recorded closed on evidence that would pass whether or not the defect returned.
findings.consequence: Not visible to the owner today — the surface currently names no bare month and speaks no studio vocabulary. The harm is to the record this round closes on: two confirmed findings are held closed by checks that would report green against the exact copy they were written to forbid, and the round's 461-assertion count overstates real coverage by eight. A regression in the movement the brief protects — a refusal written in the team's vocabulary, or a month named without its year — ships silently.
findings.fix: Edit interaction-check.mjs with an editor tool, never through a shell heredoc. At line 1250 replace `new RegExp("\\\\b" + w + "\\\\b", "i")` with `new RegExp(String.raw`\b` + w + String.raw`\b`, "i")`. At line 1231 replace `new RegExp("\\\\b" + m + "\\\\b(?!\\\\s+\\\\d{4})", "g")` with `new RegExp(String.raw`\b` + m + String.raw`\b(?!\s+\d{4})`, "g")`. Then prove each per L-06: temporarily add "the snapshot writer" to a LIMITS entry and a bare "August" to the first-run note, watch both assertions fail, restore. Finally add the self-test below so the escapes cannot be lost again.
findings.assertion: Before the page assertions, the gate self-tests its own matchers against fixed strings: the banned-vocabulary matcher applied to "The snapshot writer accrues structured periods for callers; the provider is the recorder." returns all seven banned terms, and applied to "Nothing was written down about how much was open in earlier weeks." returns none; the month matcher applied to "This arrives in August." returns ["August"] and applied to "This arrives in August 2026." returns []. Both fail the run if the matcher returns the wrong set.

findings.element: .limit .t-small (the three refusal bodies) and .note .t-body, between 561px and 900px
findings.problem: `.limit .t-small` carries no max-width at all, and `.limits` collapses to one column at `max-width: 900px`. Driven in chromium and measured by word ranges, the third refusal body sets 121 characters on a line at 900px, 118 at 899, 103 at 793 and 792, and 97 at the declared 768 viewport that has a committed frame. One pixel wider — 901px — the same paragraph sets at 30 characters, because the grid returns to three columns. The measure swings 4x across a single pixel with nothing but the column count controlling it. `.note .t-body` does declare a ceiling, 62ch, but ch is the width of the zero glyph and not a character: at 900px that 62ch resolves to 616px and still sets 90 characters on line one. At 1440 the same refusal copy sets at a well-judged 48–54 characters, which is what the design intends and what the 561–900 band never gets.
findings.consequence: In the movement the brief protects as the product's signature, the owner reads three unbroken 120-character lines of 13px type on a tablet. At that measure the return sweep loses the line — the eye cannot reliably find the start of the next one — and the refusals stop reading as designed statements and start reading as unstyled paragraph text. It is the one movement whose whole job is to be believed, and it is set worst at the width a venue owner is most likely to hold.
findings.fix: In the stylesheet, add `max-width: 42ch;` to `.limit .t-small` and `max-width: 40ch;` to `.limit .t-head`, and change `.note .t-body { max-width: 62ch }` to `max-width: 46ch`. 42ch at 13px resolves to 362px, so the ceiling never bites at 1440 (where the column is 319px) and caps the 561–900 band at roughly 55 characters — the same measure the three-column layout already delivers.
findings.assertion: For every state and at 390, 560, 768, 792, 900, 1280 and 1440, no element matching `.limit .t-small`, `.limit .t-head`, `.note .t-body`, `.center .t-body` or `.ghost-say p` sets more than 75 characters on any single line, measured by walking Range rects over the text node's words and grouping them by rounded top.

findings.problem: `text-wrap` computes to `wrap` on every element on the surface — no `balance`, no `pretty`, no non-breaking bindings anywhere. Driven across all seven states, four widths and both grounds, five distinct blocks end on a single word: the ghost plot's centred 20px caption breaks "Open work over time — the chart that would go / here", four characters centred under a 45-character line, at 768, 900, 1280 and 1440; the quiet state's centred body ends on "else." alone, 31px of a 436px measure; the empty state's centred body ends on "things." alone; the fifth KPI label ends on "else" alone at 1280 and 1440 while its four neighbours sit on one line, and at 390 the first card ends on "fortnight" alone; and the first-run note breaks the comparison date itself — "Yours arrive on 10 August / 2026." — at every one of the four declared widths. Two of the five are centred, which is where a one-word last line is most conspicuous, and both sit inside protected objects.
findings.consequence: The owner is never misled, but the surface stops looking typeset. A four-letter word alone and centred in the middle of the drawn-but-empty plot is the first thing the eye lands on in that figure, and it undercuts the argument that object exists to make. Splitting "10 August" from "2026" is worse than a plain widow: the one date a first-run owner is being told to wait for arrives in two pieces on two lines.
findings.fix: Add to the stylesheet: `.ghost-say .t-head, .center .t-sect, .center .t-body, .kpi > .t-small, .ages .band-head .t-head { text-wrap: balance; }` and `.limit .t-small, .hero-note, .note .t-body { text-wrap: pretty; }`. Separately, stop the comparison date breaking at render time rather than in the generated fixture: in the `first-run` view in lately.html, replace `${esc(D.comparisonArrives)}` with `${esc(D.comparisonArrives).replace(/ /g, "\u00a0")}`.
findings.assertion: For every state at 390, 768, 900, 1280 and 1440, every element matching `.ghost-say .t-head`, `.center .t-body`, `.kpi > .t-small`, `.ages .band-head .t-head` or `.hero-note` whose text runs to more than one line has a last line carrying either two or more words or at least 30% of the width of its own longest line; and in `first-run` the string "10 August 2026" occupies exactly one line box.

findings.element: .coverage span — the last provenance stamp, at 390
findings.problem: The stamp "Bound · workspace, owner, reading date and the 9" measures 349px of tracked uppercase mono; at 390 the page content box is 342px. It overflows by 7px and wraps, leaving the bare digit 9 alone on a second line — screenshotted at 390 in every state. `.coverage span` sets no `white-space` and the stamps have no internal break control, so the wrap point is whatever falls out. This is a typesetting claim about where the line breaks, not the round-2 claim about what the nine means. The gate's own comment above the guard at interaction-check.mjs:263 states these strings are kept "short enough for the stamp voice it is set in" and cites a 134-character string that ran too long — but the assertion beneath it only tests that the substrings "lab-authored", "Bound" and "reading date" are present. Nothing measures whether a stamp fits on one line, which is why this survived.
findings.consequence: At the width the product ships to a venue owner, the shared denominator — the one number all five KPI cards are counted out of, and a protected object — hangs alone at the foot of the reading as an unattached digit. The provenance strip is the surface's own credential; a stamp that breaks its own sentence in half reads as an accident rather than a statement.
findings.fix: Bind the tail of the stamp so it cannot break onto the digit: in `shell()` in lately.html, change `Bound workspace, owner, reading date and the ${D.open}` to `Bound workspace, owner, reading date and the ${D.open}`. The stamp then breaks after "date" and carries "and the 9" together on the second line.
findings.assertion: For every state at 390, 768, 1280 and 1440 and in both grounds, no `.coverage span` renders a line box carrying fewer than two words, and no `.coverage span` line is narrower than 24px.
